To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections from blood donors who have traveled abroad is low.

• Blood donors should be allowed to give blood if they have travelled to a region where there is no risk of malaria transmission (i.e. no risk of Plasmodium vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae or P. falciparum) • Blood donors should not be deferred for travel to a region with a low risk of malaria transmission • Blood donors should continue to be deferred if they have been to an area with a moderate or high risk of malaria transmission,

(1) the impact of climate change on the distribution of infectious diseases is a major concern for public health and blood safety; (2) the risk of blood-borne infections associated with travel is likely to increase due to globalization and climate changes; (3) a new approach to blood donor screening and pathogen reduction is needed to address the new challenges; and (4) a relaxation of the current blood donation restrictions for certain infectious diseases may be considered.

the impact of climate change and travel on emerging infectious diseases.
understanding the impact of climate change on emerging diseases.
the impact of climate change on the spread and emergence of infectious diseases, and the potential implications of climate change on human health.

a more detailed and accurate screening strategy is required to ensure the safety of blood transfusions.

the risk of blood transfusion-transmitted infections can be reduced by improving screening strategies and pathogen inactivating procedures, but the impact of global climate change will also require new strategies in selecting blood donors.
